title: Three Styles of Parenting
text:
In the 1960s, the psychologist Diana Baumrind at the University of California, Berkeley, set out to learn which kinds of parenting go along with confident, capable young children. She first observed preschoolers at nursery school over several months and sorted them by behavior: some were self-reliant, curious and content; others were withdrawn and distrustful; others had little self-control.

She then studied their parents closely, through home visits during the busy hours before dinner, structured observations and interviews. Clear patterns emerged. The parents of the most competent children were warm and involved, but also firm. They set clear rules and expected mature behavior, yet explained their reasons and listened to the child's point of view. Baumrind called this style authoritative.

Parents of the more withdrawn children tended to be controlling and less warm, stressing obedience without explanation; she called them authoritarian. Parents of the least self-controlled children were warm but made few demands and set few limits, a style she called permissive.

Later researchers added a fourth, neglectful style. Baumrind's framework became one of the most widely used in developmental psychology, and the advantage of authoritative parenting has been found in many, though not all, cultural settings.
lesson: Warmth and firmness are not opposites. Children do best with high expectations, clear limits, and reasons they can understand.
source: Baumrind, D. (1967). Child care practices anteceding three patterns of preschool behavior. Genetic Psychology Monographs, 75(1), 43-88.
caveat: The original samples were small, mostly white and middle class, and the findings are correlational, so they show association rather than proof that the parenting style caused the outcome.
